verdict.reasoning: Patient says, “Feeling very sort of breathless recently,” and doctor confirms, “you said you're a bit short of breath, is that right?”
Patient reports, “whenever I like. Breathe deeply, it sort of catches in the right hand side of my back,” consistent with pleuritic right-sided back pain on deep inspiration.
Patient states, “I coughed up a bit of blood on two occasions,” which is haemoptysis.

Doctor: “how long has this been going on for now?” Patient: “Just a day, really.” Doctor later summarizes, “in the last day or so, that's when you get the cough and the pain inside and you've coughed blood,” and patient does not object.

Patient: “I've been feeling a bit like a bit tired at work… exercising has been a bit difficult… performing daily activities has been a bit harder than usual.” When asked how long, patient says, “Only for a couple of weeks or so.”
Patient: “I've got a bit of a slight fever,” and later says they checked it “With the back of my hand,” indicating subjective fever without a measured temperature.
Patient: “I sort of feel my heart beating,” and doctor clarifies, “you can feel your heart kind of beating a bit faster, you think, than normal?” indicating palpitations/sensation of heart beating.
Patient states, “I've got sle,” and doctor repeats, “Sle. Okay.” indicating systemic lupus erythematosus.
Patient: “Yeah. Methotrexate.” Doctor asks timing: “When was the last time you had methotrexate?” Patient: “This morning.”
Doctor: “Do you have any allergies to any medication?” Patient: “No.” Also later: “Do you have any allergies to any antibiotics?” Patient: “No.”
Doctor: “Have you ever had any clots in your legs or clots in your lungs, blood clots?” Patient: “Not that I know of, no.” Doctor: “Anyone in the family have that?” Patient: “No.”
Doctor asks, “do you smoke at all?” Patient responds, “No.”
Patient: “I work in an office. Just a desk job.”
Doctor: “Do you live alone?” Patient: “Yes.” Doctor: “In a flat or a house?” Patient: “Flat.”
Doctor: “Do you have any pets?” Patient: “Cats?” Doctor: “A cat. Okay.” indicating a cat at home.

Symptoms listed (cough with haemoptysis, pleuritic right-sided back pain, subjective fever) match transcript. Doctor: “this sounds like you might have a chest infection… we do need to assess you to figure out whether you have a pneumonia or chest infection,” implying likely chest infection but need to exclude other causes.
Transcript confirms SLE and methotrexate use, but the doctor never explicitly discusses immunosuppression or increased infection risk as an assessment point; that inference is added.

Palpitations and reduced exercise tolerance are documented. Doctor plans vitals reassessment: “I would like someone to listen to your chest and check your blood pressure and to recheck your pulse as well. Just make sure. Check your temperature, make sure all those parameters are okay.”

Same-day face-to-face review is planned, and chest auscultation, BP, pulse, and temperature are explicitly mentioned. Oxygenation (e.g., O2 sats) is never mentioned: “listen to your chest and check your blood pressure and to recheck your pulse as well… Check your temperature.” Adding oxygenation contradicts the specific plan described.

Doctor: “You may well need an antibiotic… I'm not going to prescribe anything for you now because I think you need to have that basic assessment first before we proceed to the next step. But that's what I would predict the next step might be,” consistent with considering empiric antibiotics after face-to-face assessment if chest infection confirmed.

Doctor: “we might need to get some investigations to exclude [lung cancer]… we may end up having to do a follow up chest X ray if things don't settle down,” matching consideration of chest X-ray and further investigations if warranted or not improving.
Doctor explicitly says, “I'm not going to prescribe anything for you now because I think you need to have that basic assessment first,” confirming no antibiotics were prescribed in this consultation.
Doctor: “I'm going to leave the number in the notes for this appointment for you to ring our support team and then they will book you in for a face to face appointment… today.”
There is no mention of reassessing methotrexate or discussing it with the treating team in the plan; this is new information not in the transcript.
Doctor: “What I think we'll do is we'll arrange for you to get reviewed in a clinic today… book you in for a face to face appointment with one of our GPS today.”
After counting pulse, doctor says, “I think that was about 11 or 12. So that would make your heart rate about 66 to 74. That's okay.”
Doctor guides capillary refill and then states, “Okay, perfect. That's great. Thank you so much,” indicating a normal/brisk capillary refill time on video.

Doctor visually inspects throat (“If you position your device… mouth open wide… Say ah… Perfect. Thank you for that.”) but does not explicitly state that the oropharynx is normal or that there is no abnormality; this interpretation is added.
Doctor asks patient to feel neck glands; patient: “No, they feel pretty normal to me. I think.” This supports no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy by patient report.

No in-person exam occurred; doctor states that chest auscultation, BP, and measured temperature are to be done later: “someone needs to listen to your chest and maybe check your blood pressure as well… Check your temperature,” implying these measurements are not yet available.
Doctor: “examining you now, from what limited examination I could do online, everything does seem to be okay in terms of. You don't seem acutely unstable.”
